notes.meaning: After settling into their towns following the long journey home, the Israelites gathered in Jerusalem with one single heart and purpose. The seventh month on their calendar was filled with sacred feasts, and they set aside their everyday work to meet with God. Their united gathering showed that seeking God came before their personal comfort or ordinary business.

Jeshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the royal leader stepped forward to rebuild the altar for burnt offerings. An altar was a raised stone platform where sacrifices were offered to seek God's mercy and make things right with Him. They carefully followed the written Law of Moses rather than making up their own rules. They knew worship and seeking God's favor had to come before any building project.

The people set the altar right on its ancient foundation and started offering the daily morning and evening sacrifices again. Surrounding nations were hostile and frightening, but this fear drove the exiles straight to God for protection. They knew that an altar honoring God was a better defense than stone walls.

The exiles celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles, a week-long festival where Israelites lived in simple branch shelters to remember how God cared for their ancestors in the desert. They offered the exact number of daily animal sacrifices commanded in the Law for each day of the festival. For a people who had just returned to ruined homes, remembering God's faithfulness in the wilderness was especially meaningful.

Once the festival ended, the priests kept up the full schedule of daily sacrifices, monthly New Moon offerings, and all the special annual feasts. The people also brought freewill offerings, giving freely out of deep gratitude to God. Even though they had little money, their hardships had given them a burning desire to worship God generously.

Sacrifices to the Lord began right away on the first day of the seventh month, even though not a single stone of the temple foundation had yet been laid. Worship and prayer did not have to wait for a grand building to be finished. The people understood that having an altar to meet God was more urgent than having a completed house for His name.

The leaders hired local stone workers and carpenters, and they traded food, drink, and olive oil to the seacoast cities of Tyre and Sidon for precious cedar wood. These tall cedar logs were cut in Lebanon, floated down the Mediterranean Sea to the port of Joppa, and brought to Jerusalem. This copied what King Solomon had done for the first temple, made possible by the official permission given by King Cyrus of Persia.

Work on the temple building began in the spring of their second year, the very same month of the year that Solomon had begun the first temple centuries earlier. Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and all the returned exiles joined together and placed the Levites in charge of overseeing the laborers. Following the rule King David had established, Levites who were twenty years old or older were appointed to guide and encourage the work.

The leading Levitical families united as a single team to supervise and direct the builders. This Jeshua was not the high priest, but a Levite leader who worked alongside Kadmiel and Henadad. Their unified leadership gave heart and energy to all the laborers working on God's house.

As soon as the foundation stones were in place, the community held a service of praise and worship right at the construction site. Priests dressed in their sacred robes blew trumpets, while Levites from the family of Asaph crashed cymbals, exactly as King David had ordered long ago. Even with only the foundation finished, they stopped to give God the honor due to His name.

The musicians sang back and forth to each other with words of praise and thanks, repeating the ancient song that God is good and His faithful love lasts forever. When the people heard the music and saw the foundation laid, the whole crowd let out a thunderous shout of joy. They were overflowing with gratitude because God had shown mercy to His people after their long years of captivity.

Elderly priests, Levites, and family heads who were old enough to remember Solomon's glorious temple began to weep out loud when they saw this new foundation. They grieved because this new building seemed small and humble, and it lacked sacred treasures like the ark of the covenant. At the same time, younger people who had grown up in exile with no temple at all shouted with pure joy.

The weeping of the elders and the cheering of the younger generation mixed together into one massive sound that could be heard from far away. In this life, God's people often experience deep grief and high joy side by side. We should be careful not to let sorrow over the past rob us of thankfulness for what God is doing today.
